story:
Otto Suwen thinks that this is quite a troublesome situation, to his mind.

The trouble began with a slight shortage of ink in his pen tip. While out in the city to buy some, the hem of his cloak was grabbed by a single girl.

"Mommy, where...?"

The girl pleaded with tearful eyes—barely ten years old, if that, more a little child than a girl, without a doubt. To be caught by a child that age meant all was lost, he thought.

"If only she were even a bit older, things might be different..."

Judging the matter by the other party's age might be a mistake, but in moments like these, what flitted through Otto's mind was something terribly calculating: how this action would "resonate with the Emilia camp."

If word spread that Otto here wasn't being sympathetic to a little girl, it would deal a blow to the camp. He couldn't risk that—or so Otto, appointed as the camp's internal affairs officer, believed.

"I never asked for a position like this..."

Such thoughts slipped out in a sigh, but there was no one around to hear them. If they had been overheard, he could vividly imagine familiar faces and voices saying things like, "Hey, hey, Otto—judge not, that ye be not judged!" or "If Otto-kun isn't keen on it, there's nothing to be done, but that girl is hurting right now, and I think we're the only ones who can do something for her." With that in mind, Otto let out a sigh.

"I'm telling you this upfront, but the real me wouldn't go around offering help to just anyone without reservation, you know."

With those words, he starts walking, pulling the little girl along by the hand.

For today, the bustle of the Costool town's streets is undoubtedly due to the signs of the upcoming festival.

If you consider the unfamiliar, unaccustomed atmosphere of the little girl as something related to that—something that came from outside—then it all fits together.

In that case, the guardian from whom the little girl got separated is most likely waiting at a prominent spot in town—a landmark—or calling out for her.

"Got it? Remember this. If after this, you're treated kindly by strangers, and if I'm the first one to do that, then it's not thanks to me—it's thanks to the people who turned me into the kind of person who does things like this."

At those words, the little girl nodded repeatedly with teary eyes and a face that couldn't shake off its anxiety. Whether she understood the meaning or simply didn't want to be abandoned by the Otto right in front of her, that distinction was unclear.

But whichever it was—

"I'm sure the people I know would be relieved to hear that you were spared from any sorrow."
Murmuring something like that, Otto took the little girl's hand and walked through the bustling streets—crowded with people coming and going, the kind of urban sprawl where a child her age could easily get lost—while still holding her hand.
To be hit with such an unwelcome and unexpected situation, saddled with the dishonorable title of "little girl handler," which should only apply to his own friends, of all things—
"Good grief, if this sort of thing makes life any harder, that'll be a real problem."
Muttering as much while slowing his pace so the little girl wouldn't fall behind, Otto Suwen pressed on with his steps.

—It would be a little while longer before Otto realized he'd forgotten to buy ink for his pen nib, held back by the little girl making a huge fuss over reuniting with her family and her family themselves keeping him there.
